# Diagnosing Warm Engine Crank Delays: A Systematic Approach

A cold-start delay that vanishes once the engine reaches operating temperature is a classic symptom of fuel delivery or vapor lock issues, but your specific case presents an interesting variation. You have a 2008 Toyota Kluger with a V6 engine that cranks for five seconds only after sitting idle for a while during the day, yet starts instantly if you restart within three to four minutes of shutting it down. The fact that it starts perfectly after an eight-hour overnight sit rules out simple fuel starvation or a failing fuel pump priming issue.

This behavior strongly suggests the problem lies in the state of the fuel system when the vehicle has been idling, rather than when it is completely off. When you shut the engine down and restart immediately, the residual pressure in the rail keeps the injectors pressurized. However, if the car sits for a short period (say, 20 minutes) before you drive again, that residual pressure may bleed slightly, or more likely, the fuel mixture has warmed up enough to create vapor lock conditions within the lines or the pump itself.

The core issue is likely related to how the ECU manages fuel pressure and injector pulse width when transitioning from a warm-idle state back to running under load. In many modern engines, including the V6 in your Kluger, the fuel system relies on maintaining a specific residual pressure. If this pressure drops below a threshold while the engine is cool but warmed up, the ECU has to crank longer just to build enough pressure for injection.

Your diagnostic steps so far have been thorough and correctly targeted common failure points. Cleaning the mass airflow sensor (MAF) and throttle body addresses air-fuel mixture stoichiometry issues, which typically cause rough idle or stalling rather than cranking delays. Replacing spark plugs with OEM parts ensures ignition timing is sound, and using high-quality fuel eliminates contamination variables. The fact that you've run multiple cycles of fuel system cleaner while the tank was empty also clears any significant varnish buildup in the injectors themselves.

The key insight here is distinguishing between "cold start" enrichment and "warm idle" pressure retention. Since the car starts fine after 8–9 hours, the battery and alternator are clearly capable of delivering the necessary current to spin the starter motor at full RPM for an extended period without voltage sag. This eliminates the electrical side as the primary culprit.

The most probable cause is a weak fuel pump or a clogged in-line filter that can maintain pressure overnight (due to low flow demand) but struggles when the system needs to rapidly replenish volume after a short idle period where some vaporization has occurred. Another possibility, specific to older Toyota V6 architectures, is a failing fuel pressure regulator in the rail. If the regulator allows pressure to bleed off too quickly while idling, the ECU detects low pressure and attempts a longer crank to compensate, thinking the system isn't pressurized enough for injection.

To isolate this without disassembly, monitor the fuel pressure gauge during these specific intervals: check the pressure right after shutting down the car immediately versus waiting 15–20 minutes before attempting a restart. If the pressure drops significantly in the shorter window, the pump or regulator is likely the bottleneck. Addressing this ensures reliable starting behavior regardless of how long you've been parked.
